why: M1 has an exit condition that says the ground truth's four layers -- entity, fault, process, evidence -- must all be fillable. Nothing could check it: the schema marks the causal chain and the checkpoints optional, and the root-cause entity id is a string no code resolves. This file names the cases that have been annotated in all four layers, with the graph that answers their references, so the count is a measurement rather than a claim. It grows one case at a time; the guard reports how many of the thirty extraction samples carry one and refuses a case that is incomplete or whose references do not resolve. Five cases now, and each layer of each case must carry a quote, and the guard requires each quote to appear verbatim in the incident text the case was annotated from: an annotation that cannot show where it came from is an opinion about the text, and the quote is the one part of it a machine can check.

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `resource-cpu-saturation-checkout`: the container, the pod it belongs to and the service it serves are all named or implied by the text, the two causal steps are the text's own sequence (limit -> throttling -> latency), and the three checkpoints are the three numbers the text states (500m, the throttling counters, 180ms -> 4.3s). The downstream payment service is a graph node because the text names it, but it carries no checkpoint: the text says its error rate did not change, which is an absence rather than a value a checkpoint can hold.

sources.quote: the pod sat pinned at its 500m limit
sources.why: the workload whose container carries the limit -- the pod is the entity the chain passes through

sources.quote: Container CPU throttling counters climbed the whole time
sources.why: the observed mechanism, which is what makes this `resource` and `cpu-saturation` rather than a latency-only fault

sources.quote: checkout-api p99 latency went from 180ms to 4.3s over eleven minutes
sources.why: the second step's effect, and the sentence that orders it after the throttling rather than beside it

sources.quote: 180ms to 4.3s
sources.why: the two numbers the p99 checkpoint holds; a checkpoint with one number would not say what the fault changed

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `network-delay-cart-to-inventory`. This case is the one whose answer is a *comparison*: the caller's span carries 900ms and the callee's handler carries 11ms, and neither number means anything alone -- 900ms is a slow service and 11ms is a healthy one, so the fault lives in the difference. The chain is one step because the text supports one: the two services are the two entities, and the sentence that puts the time on the wire is the mechanism. The start time and the system name are declared by the corpus rather than extracted from the text, which states a policy change and no clock.

sources.quote: while the inventory service's own server-side handler time stayed at 11ms
sources.why: the callee, named as the entity whose own time did not move

sources.quote: No packet loss and no retransmits
sources.why: what rules out loss and retransmission, leaving delay as the mechanism

sources.quote: so the time is being spent on the wire
sources.why: the one sentence that locates the added time between the two processes

sources.quote: rose from 12ms to 900ms
sources.why: the two numbers the client-span checkpoint holds, and the baseline it is measured against

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `middleware-kafka-consumer-lag`. The text states the diagnosis and its own control in the same sentence: lag grew, the consumers were alive and polling, and broker throughput was unchanged with spare partitions -- so the case's chain runs from the consumer to the topic rather than the other way, and a case that pointed at the broker would be contradicted by the text's last clause. The six-hour window is the text's; the absolute start time is declared by the corpus.

sources.quote: Consumer group order-events accumulated 4.2 million messages of lag
sources.why: the consumer group is the root cause and the topic is where the lag is observed

sources.quote: their per-message processing time tripled after a schema change added a synchronous outbound call per record
sources.why: the mechanism, and the change that introduced it

sources.quote: so this is consumer-side throughput, not broker capacity
sources.why: the sentence that directs the chain from consumer to topic rather than the reverse

sources.quote: 4.2 million messages of lag over six hours
sources.why: the lag checkpoint's value and the window it accumulated over

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `middleware-queue-watermark-ledger-writer`. The mechanism lives in a configuration change one level below the workload that failed -- the topic's retention was raised to seven days on volumes sized for three -- so the chain points from the writer to its topic and the mechanism sentence carries the direction, because a graph edge that said 'the topic calls the writer' would be a topology nobody deployed. This is also the first case in the corpus that can fill a logs.csv: the broker states the watermark in its own words, so the log line is quoted rather than invented, and the export stops being a file with a header and no rows for one case out of four.

sources.quote: The ledger writer's publishes began timing out at 21:40
sources.why: the failing workload, named as the thing whose publishes stopped

sources.quote: the topic's retention was raised to seven days during the week and the broker volumes were sized for three
sources.why: the mechanism: a retention change against a volume footprint that cannot hold it

sources.quote: Producers were throttled rather than failed
sources.why: what makes this throttling and not an outage -- the writer's buffer grew instead of its publishes erroring

sources.quote: the disk watermark crossed 92 percent
sources.why: the checkpoint's value, stated by the broker rather than inferred

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `code-unhandled-exception-export`, and the corpus's first code-level case. The mechanism is an absence -- the worker never sends a nack, so the broker sees a closed connection and the job is never retried -- which is why the process layer quotes the sentence about what the broker saw rather than a sentence about the failure itself. The evidence is split deliberately: the only number the text states is the failure share, and the mechanism exists only as a log line, so the two checkpoints are a measurement and a quotation. There is no span because the text gives no duration.

sources.quote: The export worker dies mid-job and the job is never retried
sources.why: the workload, named with the property that makes it a code fault -- it dies without reporting

sources.quote: an unhandled TypeError in the CSV writer when a column contains an embedded newline
sources.why: the exception and its trigger, which is the whole mechanism in one clause

sources.quote: the broker sees the connection close rather than a nack
sources.why: the shape of the propagation: silence instead of a signal, so the failure is not retried

sources.quote: Roughly 3% of exports fail
sources.why: the only number the text states, and the checkpoint that carries it

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `config-ingress-timeout-partner-portal`, and the corpus's first `config` case and its first whose root cause is not in the application at all. The mechanism is one number against another: the ingress waits 1s for a read the handler needs about eight seconds to finish, so the two causal layers are the annotation (fault) and what the application did anyway (process -- its own logs show the work completing, which is why this is a timeout and not a crash). The evidence is split for the same reason: the only quantities the text gives are the two timeouts and the handler's need, plus the fact that 504s began, so the checkpoints are a configuration fact cited from the case's own parameters, the existence of the failures, the unchanged handler, and the log line that shows the work finishing after the client was gone. The previous value of 600s is declared beside the injected one rather than turned into a second checkpoint: it is history, not something the case ran under.

sources.quote: Partner portal uploads began failing with 504 for files over 5MB
sources.why: the service the failures are reported against, and the size threshold that scopes them

sources.quote: The annotation that sets the upstream read timeout was written as 1s where the previous value was 600s
sources.why: the configuration change itself, in both its value and the value it replaced

sources.quote: its own logs show the work completing
sources.why: what the application did while the ingress was refusing: the work finished, which turns the 504 into a timeout rather than a failure of the handler

sources.quote: the upload handler needs about eight seconds
sources.why: the duration the 1s timeout has to be compared with, and the one series that does not move

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `dependency-upstream-5xx-pricing`, and the corpus's first `dependency` case and its first whose root cause is a third party rather than a component of the system. The annotation's job here is to separate the two services the text keeps together: the pricing service is what failed, and tax-calculation is why. Every layer is chosen to make that separation: the entity layer is the dependency itself rather than the service that reported the failures, the process layer is the mechanism sentence (a 503 answered to three calls in five), and the evidence layer is a pair plus a control -- the pricing service's 502 share, the dependency's own 503 share, and the zero against every other dependency, which is the sentence that rules the reporting service out. The share the injection declares is also a checkpoint, so the number in `fault.parameters` and the number in the telemetry have to agree rather than being two statements nobody compares.

sources.quote: Every failure is an upstream tax-calculation call answering 503
sources.why: the component the failures come from, which is the answer the case is asking for

sources.quote: The tax provider's status page shows a degradation window that matches exactly
sources.why: the fault as the provider states it, with a window that lines up with the symptom rather than merely preceding it

sources.quote: The pricing service returned 502 on 60% of requests for 18 minutes
sources.why: what the system did with the upstream's answers, which is the step that turns a dependency failure into a user-visible one

sources.quote: the pricing service's own error rate against all other dependencies is zero
sources.why: the control that localises the fault to one upstream, and the one number that is a zero rather than a share

cases.why: annotated from the incident text of `runtime-container-crash-loop-media`: the corpus's first `runtime` case, and the first whose window is a number the text states rather than one the corpus chose. That is the whole point of it: '178 times in 12 hours' cannot be declared in a half-hour window, and until the cadence followed the window it could not be declared at all. The four layers separate the crash from the probe: entity is the container, fault is the segfault in the native binding, process is the pod never reaching a state where a probe can pass, and evidence is the counter the text gives plus the flat zero the second sentence implies. The probe ratio is deliberately a checkpoint at exactly zero -- it is the sentence that rules the liveness probe out, and a case that could not state a zero could not state that.

sources.quote: The media-transcoder container has restarted 178 times in 12 hours
sources.why: the workload, named with the count that makes the window twelve hours

sources.quote: logs a segmentation fault in the native ffmpeg binding within two seconds of receiving the first job
sources.why: the fault itself, with the timing that shows it happens on every start

sources.quote: before the HTTP listener comes up, so no probe ever passes
sources.why: the propagation: the process is gone before anything could probe it, which is why this is a crash loop rather than a failing probe

sources.quote: Liveness probes are not the cause: the exits all predate the probe window
sources.why: the sentence that excludes the probe as the cause, and the one the zero checkpoint rests on
